title: Akshay Kumar Turns Villain, Saif Ali Khan Plays the Hero — and Priyadarshan Has Reunited Them After 18 Years
excerpt: The 'Haiwaan' release date is locked for September 11, Mohanlal has a surprise cameo, and the non-theatrical deal already has the trade buzzing at ₹80 crore.
body:
There's a poster circulating on the internet today that deserves your attention. Two men, two vastly different energies, one word between them: **Haiwaan**. On one side, **Akshay Kumar** — jaw clenched, fists tight, radiating something darker than anything we've seen from him in years. On the other, **Saif Ali Khan** — cooler, sharper, the man who'll have to stop whatever Akshay's character is about to unleash. Between them stands the quiet confidence of a filmmaker who's done this before: **Priyadarshan**.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=UmFDaTemk4E</youtube>

The release date dropped this morning, and it landed like a gauntlet: **September 11, 2026**. Mark it.

> "One obsession. One relentless pursuit. One date you'll want to remember." — KVN Productions

Let's start with the headline act. Akshay Kumar is playing an antagonist. Not the loveable rogue he's perfected in a dozen comedies, not the patriotic hero of his earnest dramas — a full-blown villain. He's spoken about it himself, calling the role one that "pushed, shaped, and surprised" him. And if the intense first-look video he shared from the final schedule is anything to go by — black car, clenched fist, murder in his eyes — this isn't a wink-and-nod bad guy. This is a man who has decided to be terrifying.

Saif, meanwhile, brings the polish. Their on-set dynamic is already the stuff of legend. Akshay described it best: **"Saif's humour is very 'SoBo' (South Bombay), while mine is more Andheri and Borivali."** That line alone tells you what kind of chemistry to expect — effortless, electric, two actors who genuinely enjoy being around each other.

The two haven't shared a frame since **Tashan** in 2008 — a film that, let's be diplomatic, didn't exactly set the Ganges on fire. But eighteen years is a long time, both men have evolved into entirely different artists, and Priyadarshan is the kind of director who knows how to weaponise star power. This is his **eighth collaboration with Akshay**, and their recent pairing on **Bhooth Bangla** proved the old magic hadn't just survived — it had matured.

**Haiwaan** is inspired by Priyadarshan's own 2016 Malayalam film **Oppam**, which starred **Mohanlal** in one of his most celebrated performances. But "inspired" is the operative word here — the dialogues and screenplay have been reworked, the tone has shifted, and the Hindi version promises to be its own animal entirely. Speaking of Mohanlal: he's doing a cameo. Priyadarshan confirmed it with a grin and a tease — **"His character will definitely be a surprise for the audience."** When a director describes a Mohanlal appearance as a "surprise," you pay attention.

The supporting cast reads like a filmmaker who's building an ensemble, not filling seats. **Shriya Pilgaonkar** brings her quiet intensity, **Saiyami Kher** adds physical grace and grit, and **Boman Irani** handles whatever register you need him to — comedy, menace, heartbreak. **Asrani**, the veteran of a hundred comedies, rounds out a cast that feels deliberately eclectic.

The trade is already paying attention. Non-theatrical rights — satellite, digital, and music — have reportedly been acquired by **Sony Network for approximately ₹80 crore**, meaning the producers have recovered close to 70% of their investment before a single ticket is torn. That's not just confidence from the buyers; it's a signal that Haiwaan is being treated as an event film, not a mid-tier release.

For the Indian diaspora, this is the kind of Bollywood film that used to pack out Leicester Square and Sunnyvale AMCs on opening night — a proper star vehicle with genre ambitions. With Pritam handling the music (he was tagged in the official announcement) and Priyadarshan behind the camera, Haiwaan has the ingredients of both a critical conversation piece and a commercial blockbuster.

Here's the thing about September: it's traditionally a soft month for Bollywood. Alpha will have come and gone by then, the monsoon theatrical slump will be setting in, and audiences will be hungry for something that doesn't require a franchise decoder ring. Haiwaan slots into that gap perfectly — a standalone thriller with two of Hindi cinema's biggest names doing something they've never quite done together.

Akshay Kumar as the beast. Saif Ali Khan as the man who hunts him. Priyadarshan pulling the strings.

September 11. You've been warned.
